title: Mini-Ofrenda Competition
summary: Build a small ofrenda (altar) that honors someone who has died, using the traditional elements of Día de Muertos and your own creativity. Four judges score every entry with this rubric. The top three win prizes.

facts.label: Judging
facts.value: Wednesday, November 4, 2026, during the Día de Muertos event

facts.label: Prizes
facts.value: 1st: LEGO Botanicals Rocking Plants. 2nd: Hug-A-Lumps capybara plush. 3rd: Hello Kitty plush.

requirements.text: Your ofrenda fits on a base no larger than 12 × 12 inches.
It honors someone who has died: a family member, friend, pet, or a historical or public figure. Never a living person.
At least 4 elements carry a small label in Spanish (for example, “el agua: para la sed del alma”), plus a card in Spanish of 3–5 sentences: who it honors and why.
No open flames. Use LED candles. Copal and incense stay unlit.
No alcohol, tobacco, or food that can spoil. Use replicas, sealed packages or pictures for drinks and favorite foods.
Keep it a remembrance, not Halloween: no jack-o’-lanterns, witches, zombies, fake blood or costume stereotypes.
It is your own work. Store-bought pieces are fine; what you make yourself counts toward craftsmanship.
Put your name only on the back of the base. Judges see an entry number, not your name.

disqualifiers: Open flame, alcohol, tobacco or spoiling food on the ofrenda.
Content that mocks the tradition or the person honored.
Work that is not the student’s own.

scale.points_rule: Each judge scores each area 1–4. Your score is the average of the judges’ totals.

criteria.name: Traditional elements
criteria.question: Are the essential elements there, and used the way the tradition uses them?

levels.1: Few or no traditional elements; reads as general decoration.
levels.2: 2–3 traditional elements, or elements used in a way the tradition would not.
levels.3: 4–5 traditional elements, used correctly. One of the four natural elements is missing or token.
levels.4: 6 or more traditional elements, including the four natural elements: water (agua), earth (food, flowers), fire (candles) and wind (papel picado). Each is placed with purpose, e.g. marigold petals leading to the altar.

criteria.name: Meaning, explained in Spanish
criteria.question: Do the Spanish labels and card show the student understands why each element is there?

levels.2: Labels give names only, or the card is very short.
levels.3: Labels and card are present and mostly explain meaning; some labels give only the name.
levels.4: Labels on 4+ elements give the name and its purpose in Spanish; the card (3–5 sentences) clearly says who is honored and why. Spanish is clear even with small errors.

criteria.name: Personal tribute
criteria.question: Do we come away knowing something about the person being remembered?

levels.2: Honoree is named but the ofrenda could be for anyone.
levels.3: Honoree is clear, with a few personal details.
levels.4: A clear portrait of one person (or pet or figure): their photo or image, favorite foods or drinks (as replicas), objects tied to their life, details only they would have.

criteria.name: Composition and design
criteria.question: Does it work as a small altar: levels, balance, color, a focal point?

levels.2: Elements are present but crowded or scattered.
levels.3: Organized and balanced; levels or focal point present but less developed.
levels.4: Strong layout within the 12 × 12 base: levels (niveles) or tiers used with intention, balanced arrangement, a clear focal point on the honoree, a deliberate color palette.

criteria.name: Creativity and originality
criteria.question: Is there a fresh idea, an inventive material, or a personal way of telling the story?

levels.2: Mostly a standard or kit-like ofrenda.
levels.3: Some original touches on a familiar layout.
levels.4: A memorable, original idea that still respects the tradition: inventive materials, a theme drawn from the honoree’s life, handmade miniatures, surprising details.

criteria.name: Craftsmanship and care
criteria.question: Is it well made, sturdy, and finished with care?

levels.3: Well made, with minor rough spots.
levels.4: Carefully made and finished; stable; handmade pieces (papel picado, paper or tissue marigolds, miniature food) show real effort.

tiebreakers: Higher combined score on Traditional elements + Meaning in Spanish.
Then higher score on Personal tribute.
Then a show of hands by the four judges.

judging.how: Each judge scores every entry on their own, by entry number, from a phone. Each criterion gets a level from 1 to 4. An entry’s final score is the average of the judges’ totals. The three highest averages win 1st, 2nd and 3rd.

essential_elements.meaning: Quenches the thirst of the souls after their long journey; also a sign of purity.
Their light guides the souls back home. (Use LED candles in the Lab.)
An Indigenous incense whose smoke cleanses the space. (Keep it unlit.)
An Indigenous flower whose color and scent show the souls the way; petals often make a path.
The bread offered as a welcome to family and friends.
Represents the wind and the fragility of life.
What the honoree loved, offered to welcome them (replicas in the Lab).
Things tied to the person’s life, work or hobbies.
Two levels for heaven and earth; three add the underworld; seven for the steps of the soul’s journey.

notes_for_organizers: Criteria follow those used in Mexican altar contests (tradition, theme elements, creativity, craftsmanship; e.g. UPAEP and UAQ convocatorias), adapted for a 12 × 12 classroom entry and Spanish-language learning. Safety and respect rules reflect a campus setting.
